finding: On 1991-2026 history, more leverage always won: S&P 500 + SMA10 at 3x made 24.5%/yr (max DD -66%). But the forward simulation at today's valuations showed leverage does not raise the median.
decision: Leverage should follow the expected premium (Kelly: f = premium / variance). Try valuation-scaled leverage; widen leverage grids; lever the bond sleeve alone.
sources: Gayed & Bilello (2016) Leverage for the Long Run; Kelly (1956)

finding: Valuation-Kelly had the best TRAIN growth (13.8%/yr) but delevered through the 1991-2026 bull (test 14.9%). Expected wealth rises with leverage while median growth peaks near 2x (S&P+SMA10) or 2.5-3x (60/40+SMA10).
decision: Map the expected-value frontier so the leverage choice is explicit. Rank only strategies an ordinary margin account can hold (<=2x) separately from futures-only ones.
sources: Harvey et al. (2018) The Impact of Volatility Targeting; Ayres & Nalebuff, Lifecycle Investing

finding: Deployable champion: S&P 500 + SMA10 x2: 14.4%/yr since 1957, 18.1% on the untouched test period, max DD -47%, a 1987-style crash day costs -41%. Forward at CAPE 41: median 4.3%/yr (best of the frontier), mean wealth 1.83x in 10 years.
decision: Start forward paper accounts (deployable champion, research champion 60/40+SMA10 x3, 60/40 benchmark). Next: alternative trend signals under leverage, financing via leveraged ETFs (daily-reset decay), regime-specific leverage caps.

finding: Drawdown brake (test 21.2% vs 24.5% for plain 3x) and levered dual momentum (train picked 1x) lost. Seasonal leverage (3x Nov-Apr, 1x May-Oct) had the best TRAIN growth of any levered strategy (12.4%) and a smaller crash-day loss, but Sell-in-May largely vanished after its 2002 publication (t = 0.42 for 2003-2026). Valuation-scaled leverage to 3x: 15.7% test, max DD -42%.
decision: Champion unchanged. Seasonality goes on a watch list, not into the portfolio. Next: model leveraged-ETF daily-reset costs exactly with daily data, lifecycle de-leveraging, and combining the valuation and trend signals in one leverage rule.
sources: Bouman & Jacobsen (2002) The Halloween Indicator; Antonacci (2014) Dual Momentum Investing

finding: Recovery leverage (S&P 500 at 2x above its 10-month average, 3x while still >15% below its 36-month high) beat the 2x champion in training (11.6% vs 10.6%) and test (19.0% vs 18.1%), in all 12 depth/boost settings, with a higher forward median, higher average wealth and a lower chance of a 10-year loss. Variance management (Moreira-Muir) raised test growth only with more leverage and a lower forward median. Exp 16: a 2x/3x daily-reset S&P ETF matches cheap margin (+1.5%) and clearly beats retail margin (+5%), so up to 3x is reachable without a margin loan.
decision: New champion: recovery leverage (2x/3x via SSO/UPRO-style ETFs, cash otherwise). Added a 'deployable via ETFs' flag. Opened a forward paper account for it; the old 2x account continues as the margin champion. Next: when to exit faster in crashes (daily signal with a band), and a stock/bond version of recovery leverage.
sources: Moreira & Muir (2017) Volatility-Managed Portfolios; Poterba & Summers (1988); Exp 6, Exp 16

finding: Two changes to recovery leverage each beat it. (1) Exit only when BOTH the 10-month average and 12-month momentum turn down ('either' keeps you in): train 11.7% vs 11.6%, test 21.8% vs 19.0%, 125 vs 187 switches; pre-1957 roughly neutral (13.3% vs 13.0% in 1880-1929, 8.1% vs 8.4% in 1930-56). (2) Hold Treasuries instead of cash when out: train up to 13.2%. Combined (train-picked: 'either' + 2x bonds when out): train 13.6%, test 22.5%, 1957-2026 18.1%, forward median 6.8% vs 4.3%, average wealth 2.30x vs 1.89x, P(10-year loss) 14.5% vs 20.5%. COST: worst year -39% vs -30%, and 2022 -35% vs -10% (slower exit, then bonds fell with stocks). In the full-cost 5-year simulation it made 16.6%/yr vs 19.9% for the previous champion, max drawdown -41% vs -22%. A stock/bond recovery mix (0.8 stocks, 2x, 4x boost) tested 17.6%: lower growth, smaller crash-day loss (-33%).
decision: New champion by the loop rule (beats on test and forward median): recovery+ = 2x S&P (3x after >15% falls) while the S&P is above its 10-month average OR up over 12 months; 2x 7-10y Treasuries (UST) otherwise. The previous champion keeps its paper account for comparison. Watch item: stock-bond correlation regimes (2022, 1970s) are this rule's weak spot. Next: a bond-trend gate on the off-asset (hold bonds only when bonds are above their own 10-month average), then lifecycle de-leveraging.
sources: Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen (2012) Time Series Momentum; Alpha Architect (2016) What is the best risk-off asset for trend followers; CXO Advisory, Intrinsic momentum or SMA for avoiding crashes

finding: User: the algorithm must not depend on particular past years; it will trade unseen data. Audit: 219 variants have been tried against the same 1991-2026 test. A walk-forward simulation of the selection process itself (each year pick the best strategy on data known then) earned 14.9%/yr on 1991-2026 vs 22.5% for the hand-picked recovery+ champion. Most of that gap is hindsight. PSR that recovery+ has a higher Sharpe than the S&P: 0.86 (not significant). Eras never used for selection: recovery strategies made only ~8.7%/yr in 1930-1956 (≈ S&P 8.8%) because the post-crash 3x boost was caught in the false recoveries of 1930-32, while 2x/3x trend and valuation-scaled leverage made 12-19%. An equal-weight ensemble of three published effects (3x trend, valuation-scaled leverage ≤3x, recovery+) made 15.4% / 14.6% / 13.1% / 21.3% in the four eras (worst 13.1% vs 8.7% for recovery+). Forward 10-year: median 4.7%, average wealth 1.98x, P(loss) 17.5%. Full-cost 5 years: 19.9%/yr, max drawdown -26%, $398 trading costs.
decision: New champion: equal-weight ensemble (3x trend + valuation + recovery+), no fitted weights. New champion rule: rank by WORST era across 1880-1929, 1930-1956, 1957-1990 and 1991-2026; a challenger must not lose to the incumbent in any era (research.beats_everywhere); round-number, literature parameters only; the walk-forward selection return is reported as the honest estimate of what the loop itself can deliver. The only truly unseen data is the forward paper record from 2026-09. Data gap: the valuation sleeve needs monthly S&P earnings after 2023-06 (currently frozen at the last value).
sources: Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado & Zhu (2014) The Probability of Backtest Overfitting; Harvey & Liu (2015) Backtesting; Campbell & Shiller (1988); Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen (2012); Poterba & Summers (1988)

finding: Two published whipsaw cures failed the worst-era rule. Growth-trend timing (obey the 10-month trend only when 12-month earnings growth, lagged 3 months, is negative): 2x gives 9.8% / 14.7% / 7.9% / 20.2% by era, max drawdown -75%. In 1973-74 earnings were still growing in nominal terms, so it stayed invested at 2x through the crash. This matches Newfound Research's mixed results outside the US. Multi-horizon trend (1/3/12-month TSMOM, Hurst-Ooi-Pedersen 2017) on one market at 3x: 10.4% / 16.4% / 9.5% / 20.2%, worse than the plain 10-month average in 3 of 4 eras; the 1-month signal adds noise. As ensemble sleeves, worst era 11.8% (growth-trend) and 12.3% (4 sleeves) vs the champion's 13.1%. Variants tried so far: 228. Walk-forward selection estimate unchanged: 14.3%/yr 1957-2026, 14.9% 1991-2026. Infrastructure: the real-time simulation stalled when FRED published the S&P close before the 10-year yield; the yield is now carried forward (a later change is booked when it becomes known).
decision: Champion unchanged (ensemble: 3x trend + valuation + recovery+, worst era 13.1%). Both ideas go to the explored list. Multi-horizon trend may still work across MANY markets (its published setting), which needs more data. Next: (1) diversify the trend sleeve across markets once data is reachable (FRED has gold, oil, dollar index and international indices); (2) a daily crash exit for the trend sleeve, tested on FRED daily S&P 2016-2026 plus the DJIA 2007-2016 file; (3) lifecycle / fixed-fraction de-leveraging.
sources: Philosophical Economics (2016) Growth and Trend; Newfound Research (2019) Global Growth-Trend Timing; Hurst, Ooi & Pedersen (2017) A Century of Evidence on Trend-Following Investing

finding: Exp 18, daily exits for the 3x trend sleeve (Gayed & Bilello 2016), daily 2007-2026 (DJIA to 2016 chained to the FRED S&P 500, T-bills from FRED, 5bp per switch). CAGR / max DD: monthly 10-month average 14.1% / -64%; daily 200-day 15.9% / -55%; daily 200-day with ±2% band 16.5% / -58%; monthly + daily emergency exit 11.7% / -56%; 3x buy & hold 16.4% / -94%. The banded daily rule beat the monthly rule in both halves (11.7% vs 11.1% in 2007-16, 21.6% vs 17.2% in 2017-26). It cut 2022 from -54% to -41%, but lost 8.6% in 2020 (sold in the March crash, re-entered late). The emergency exit was worst: it cut 2022 losses but whipsawed otherwise.
decision: No champion change. One daily era can't pass the worst-era rule, and daily data before 2007 is not available offline. The banded daily 200-day rule (3x) joins the real-time simulation as a NEW account, checked every trading day (live_sim gained a daily mode). If it keeps up in real time AND long daily history becomes available, test it as the ensemble's trend sleeve. Next: multi-market trend data (FRED NIKKEI225 since 1949, trade-weighted dollar, oil) and lifecycle de-leveraging.
sources: Gayed & Bilello (2016) Leverage for the Long Run (Dow Award paper); Exp 13 (banded 200-day)

finding: Exp 19, an out-of-sample MARKET: the Nikkei 225, 1950-2026 (FRED, month-ends, +1.5% dividends, US T-bill cash). No rule was designed on it, and it boomed to 1989 then fell -80% over 20 years. Same rules, nothing re-fitted. Buy & hold 1x: 10.3%/yr, max DD -75%. 10-month average 1x: 9.7%, -38%, roughly flat through the 1990-2012 bust. The 10-month average at 2x made 12.7% with a -77% drawdown; at 3x 12.9% with -94%. Recovery+ 11.1% with -97%. Buy & hold 3x was wiped out. A champion-like mix (valuation sleeve replaced by a neutral 1x trend sleeve, since Japan has no earnings data) lost up to -87%; with trend 2x and recovery 1-1.5x the worst fall was -61%. Lesson: the trend filter travels (halves drawdowns out of sample), but 3x leverage relies on the strong US drift. In a long sideways bust with whipsaws, the cost of being wrong at 3x compounds toward ruin. US eras for the lower-leverage ensemble (trend 2x, recovery 1-1.5x, 1x bonds when out): 12.5% / 12.9% / 11.7% / 15.8%, worst era 11.7% vs 13.1% for the champion; max DD -39% vs -53%; crash day -33% vs -47%; forward median 4.3% vs 4.7%, average wealth 1.72x vs 1.98x, P(10-year loss) 8% vs 18%.
decision: Champion unchanged under the current rule (US worst era). The trade-off (about 1.4 points a year of worst-era growth and lower expected wealth, for far better survival in a Japan-style market) is a risk-appetite choice for the owner, reported to them. The lower-leverage ensemble joins the real-time simulation as a NEW account. Protocol addition: champion candidates now also report a Japan stress test (Exp 19) for their testable sleeves. Next: international markets on FRED for more out-of-sample tests; a valuation proxy for Japan (dividend yield) if data can be found.
sources: FRED NIKKEI225; Gayed & Bilello (2016); Faber (2007); Exp 6 (US drift)

finding: Exp 20: the US rules on 12 other markets (OECD monthly share-price indices on FRED: DE, GB, FR, IT, CA, AU, NL, CH, SE, ES, KR, JP; mostly 1950s-2026; +3% dividends; US T-bill cash; nothing re-fitted). Median growth / worst country's growth / median max DD / worst max DD. Buy & hold 9.4% / 7.2% / -59% / -69%. Trend 1x 8.6% / 7.3% / -39% / -48%: the filter halves drawdowns everywhere, as in the US. Trend 2x 10.7% / 7.5% / -75% / -88%. Trend 3x 12.0% / 4.5% / -94%, wiped out in Australia (1987 crash at 3x on monthly data); worse than -80% in all 12 markets. Recovery+ 11.2% / 8.1% / -80% / -92%. Champion-like mix (valuation sleeve replaced by a neutral 1x trend sleeve) 11.2% / 7.9% / -75% / -89%, worse than -80% in 2 of 12. Lower-leverage mix 9.7% / 7.9% / -52% / -66%, none worse than -80%. Out of sample, the champion's structure beats buy & hold in 11 of 12 markets, by +1.8 points a year at the median. Its deep drawdowns are the price, and its worst-country growth equals that of the lower-leverage mix. With daily-reset ETFs, a sleeve cannot fall below zero, so the ensemble cannot go negative even where margin-financed 3x would.
decision: Champion unchanged. On expected growth (the owner's objective) the 3x structure wins out of sample too (median 11.2% vs 9.7%), and it never hit ruin as a 3-sleeve ensemble. The 12-market test is added to the protocol: candidates report median growth, worst-country growth and worst drawdown across the 12 markets; a candidate that goes to zero in any market is excluded. The leverage question (champion vs lower-leverage ensemble) stays with the owner; both run in the real-time simulation.
sources: OECD Main Economic Indicators share prices via FRED (SPASTT01*); Exp 19

finding: Exp 21, a global trend sleeve: 13 markets (US + the 12 of Exp 20; OECD monthly, +3% dividends, USD-hedged approximation). Each market held while above its own 10-month average, equal weight, fixed rules. 1961-2026 at 3x: 15.4%/yr, max DD -65%, vs 13.8% / -71% for the US alone (same data source). Better in 1961-90 (14.3% vs 9.8%), slightly worse in 1991-2026 (16.4% vs 17.2%). At 1x: 9.1% with max DD -23% (13-market buy & hold: 10.0%, -49%). At 2x: 12.7% / -44%. Inside the champion (sleeves combined at the return level, 1961-2026): global 3x sleeve 14.7% / 18.8% / 16.9%, max DD -50%, worst year -25%. Champion: 13.8% / 21.2% / 17.8%, -53%, -30%. Global 2x sleeve: 14.0% / 17.3% / 15.8%, -45%. 4 sleeves (US + global): 14.3% / 20.4% / 17.6%, -54%.
decision: No champion change: the global sleeve loses 1991-2026 (fails beats_everywhere) and cannot be tested before 1960. It is also harder to implement: 3x on 12 foreign markets needs futures or margin, since there are no daily-reset 3x ETFs for most countries. Kept as evidence that trend plus leverage is not a US-only artefact: diversified across 13 markets it earns more, with shallower falls, over 1961-2026. Next: a deployable 2x global sleeve via country ETFs on margin; ETF data needs a source.
sources: Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen (2012); Hurst, Ooi & Pedersen (2017); Faber (2007) A Quantitative Approach to Tactical Asset Allocation; OECD MEI share prices via FRED

finding: Data bug found and fixed. The Shiller file (datasets/s-and-p-500) stopped publishing the 10-year yield, CPI and CAPE in 2023-09 and earnings in 2023-06; only prices and dividends kept updating. The loader carried them forward, so for 2023-2026: (1) bond total returns and the cash rate used a frozen 4.09% yield (real 10-year yield rose to 5.0%); (2) the valuation sleeve saw CAPE 30.8 instead of about 41, so it held 1.27x stocks instead of 0.99x and the live champion was at 2.09x instead of 2.00x. Fix: scripts/update_data.py now saves monthly FRED series (GS10, CPIAUCSL, TB3MS, CP) to data/fred_monthly.csv; the loader splices them in after Shiller's last real update (CPI rescaled at the splice; earnings extended by corporate-profit growth lagged 5 months, which errs toward a higher CAPE; CAPE recomputed Shiller's way: median error vs his published CAPE -0.2%, max 1.1% over 1900-2023). Every loop iteration was rerun: the champion's eras are 15.4% / 14.6% / 13.1% / 21.2% (test was 21.3%), worst era 13.1%, unchanged. 5-year full-cost simulation: champion 19.6%/yr (was 19.9%), 60/40 6.9% (was 7.5%; bonds now lose as yields rose), S&P 500 13.1%.
decision: Champion unchanged. Data fix committed. The real-time simulation picks up the corrected valuation signal at its next rebalance (2026-11-02); its past is untouched. Lesson for the loop: check every input series for staleness (last real change), not just the price.
sources: FRED GS10, CPIAUCSL, TB3MS, CP; Shiller (2015) Irrational Exuberance data notes

finding: Exp 22, a leverage frontier: the champion's structure scaled by one dial (0.33x to 1x), across 13 markets out of sample (US + 12 OECD; valuation sleeve stood in by a neutral 1x trend sleeve abroad; each sleeve capped at -100% like a daily-reset ETF) and on US history. Median growth / average log growth across markets / worst market / worst max DD / US worst era. 0.33x: 7.5% / 7.8% / 6.7% / -32% / 7.0%. 0.50x: 8.7% / 9.2% / 7.5% / -52% / 9.4%. 0.67x: 9.7% / 10.4% / 7.9% / -67% / 11.4%. 0.83x: 10.6% / 11.4% / 8.1% / -78% / 12.3%. 1.00x (champion): 11.2% / 12.2% / 7.9% / -85% / 13.0%. Expected (log) growth in an unseen market still rises at the champion's leverage, so the growth-optimal (Kelly) point is at or above it. But the worst market's growth peaks around 0.83x, and each step up costs about 7-13 points of worst drawdown. No market was ruined at any scale.
decision: Champion unchanged: for the owner's objective (highest expected long-run growth, no ruin) the champion's leverage is supported out of sample. Its expected growth in an unseen market is the highest tested (about 12%/yr on log terms), with no ruin in 13 markets. If the owner prefers protection against the worst case, about 0.83x of the champion maximises worst-market growth (8.1%), at -78% worst drawdown instead of -85%. Leverage beyond the champion is not tested: the trend sleeve above 3x cannot be held with ETFs.
sources: Kelly (1956); Thorp (2006) The Kelly criterion in blackjack, sports betting and the stock market; Exp 20

finding: Exp 23, country momentum rotation (Asness, Moskowitz & Pedersen 2013) across 13 markets (OECD monthly, as in Exp 21). Rule fixed in advance: top 4 by 12-1 month return, equal weight, each gated by its 10-month average. 1x: 13.8% / 9.0% / 11.2% for 1961-90 / 1991-2026 / 1961-2026, max DD -23%, vs 9.8% / 8.3% / 8.9% and -23% for the equal-weight global trend sleeve. 3x: 20.2% vs 15.1% for 1961-2026, max DD -67% vs -65%. Robust to the number held (top 2 to 6 all beat all-13 in every sub-period). Decay: the excess over all-13 was about +4.0 points a year in 1961-90, +0.8 in 1991-2013 and +0.7 in 2014-2026 (after publication), consistent with McLean & Pontiff (2016). Turnover about 4x a year at 1x.
decision: No champion change. There is no data before 1960, so the worst-era rule cannot be applied; the post-publication edge is small (+0.7 points a year); and implementation needs about 12 country ETFs plus leverage via margin. Recorded as the strongest non-US idea so far; if a deployable global sleeve is built (open direction), use momentum-ranked markets rather than equal weight. The OECD indices are monthly averages, which can flatter momentum. The 12-1 skip and one-month execution lag guard against this, but month-end data would be needed to confirm.
sources: Asness, Moskowitz & Pedersen (2013) Value and Momentum Everywhere, Journal of Finance; McLean & Pontiff (2016) Does Academic Research Destroy Stock Return Predictability?; Antonacci (2014) Dual Momentum Investing

finding: Round 10. (1) Risk-parity sleeve weights (inverse 36-month volatility of each sleeve's own returns; Qian 2005, Asness-Frazzini-Pedersen 2012): 15.2% / 14.8% / 13.1% / 19.7% by era, worst 13.1% (ties the champion), max DD -52%, crash day -46%. It loses 1.5 points a year in 1991-2026, because it underweights the 3x trend sleeve. (2) Adding variance-managed stocks (Moreira-Muir 2017) as a 4th equal sleeve: 15.4% / 15.2% / 12.5% / 21.7%, worst era 12.5% (below 13.1%), crash day -50%. Variants tried: 230.
decision: Champion unchanged: neither passes beats_everywhere. Equal weight remains the best way to combine the sleeves, consistent with DeMiguel, Garlappi & Uppal (2009): 1/N is hard to beat out of sample.
sources: Qian (2005) Risk Parity Portfolios; Asness, Frazzini & Pedersen (2012) Leverage Aversion and Risk Parity; Moreira & Muir (2017); DeMiguel, Garlappi & Uppal (2009) Optimal Versus Naive Diversification

finding: Exp 24, model risk: synthetic 70-year histories resampled from real 1957-2026 monthly returns, 200 paths. Median growth (5th percentile), structure DESTROYED (i.i.d.) vs KEPT (24-month blocks). S&P 1x: 10.6% (8.2%) vs 10.7% (7.9%). S&P 3x buy & hold: 17.7% (9.2%) vs 18.0% (8.3%). Trend 3x sleeve: 13.9% (5.3%) vs 17.5% (10.1%). Champion: 13.3% (7.3%) vs 16.3% (10.8%). P(champion beats S&P 1x): 84% without structure, 99.5% with it. With structure the champion has the best bad case of all (5th percentile 10.8% vs 8.3% for 3x buy & hold); without structure its timing costs about 3 points a year against plain leverage. Caveat: resampling only from 1957+ omits the 1929-32 crash, where 3x buy & hold was wiped out; real history (worst-era rule, Exp 20) is much harsher on plain leverage than these paths.
decision: No champion change. Model-risk statement for the owner: about two-thirds of the champion's excess over the S&P comes from leverage and one-third from timing (trend + recovery). If markets stopped trending, the champion would still beat the S&P most of the time (84%), but would lag plain leverage. Watch item for the real-time simulation: the trend sleeve's whipsaw costs are the first sign of a no-trend regime. Next: a whipsaw monitor in the weekly report (count of trend-signal flips in the past 12 months vs the historical norm).
sources: Politis & Romano (1994) stationary bootstrap; Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen (2012)

finding: Built the whipsaw monitor planned in checkpoint 17. The weekly report now counts flips of the 10-month trend signal in the last 12 completed months (Shiller history spliced with FRED month-ends) and compares them with 1957-2026: average 1.3 flips per 12 months, 90th percentile 3. Now: 2 flips, normal; signal in (September 2026 month-end). More than 3 flips is flagged as a possible trendless market, the condition under which Exp 24 shows the champion lags plain leverage.
decision: No strategy change. The monitor is an early-warning input for the weekly learning review, not a trading rule. Acting on it would be a new strategy and would have to pass the worst-era rule like any other.
sources: Exp 24; Hurst, Ooi & Pedersen (2017) on trend-following drawdowns in trendless periods

finding: Capital-gains tax added to the execution simulator (execution.simulate(tax_rate=...)): a flat rate on each year's net realized gains, losses carried forward, paid from cash the next January, plus the value after selling everything at the end. 5-year full-cost simulation (2021-10 to 2026-09, $100k) at 25%. Champion: $10,372 tax paid along the way; $245,003 pre-tax becomes $207,278 if sold (15.7%/yr after tax vs 19.6% pre-tax). S&P 500 buy & hold: no tax until sold; $184,899 becomes $163,673 (10.4%/yr vs 13.1%). 60/40: 5.4% vs 6.9%. Recovery+ challenger: 13.1% after tax. Tax costs the champion about 3.9 points a year (it realizes gains at each switch) against 2.7 for buy & hold, but its lead stays about 5 points a year after tax.
decision: Reporting change, no strategy change. The dashboard's 5-year table now shows tax paid and after-tax results. The actual rate depends on the owner's country and account type (a tax-deferred account would remove the drag). Taxes favour buy-and-hold structures; a future candidate could cut realized gains by rebalancing less often (e.g. a ±10% band instead of monthly).
sources: Israel Tax Authority capital-gains rate 25%; US IRS long-term 15-20% / short-term ordinary rates; Jeffrey & Arnott (1993) Is Your Alpha Big Enough to Cover Its Taxes?
